full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim J : On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, rule was issued on 341-2016 calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar, in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 arising out of CR Case No. 847 of 2013 of the Senior Judicial Magistrate Court, Sadar, Cox's Bazar convicting the petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him to suffer simple imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Taka 1,60,00,000 (one crore sixty lac) should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The relevant facts for the purpose of disposal of the rule, are that, on 1-8-2013 the opposite party No. 2 as complainant filed CR Case No. 847 of 2013 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 before the Senior Judicial Magistrate Court, Cox's Bazar Sadar, Cox's Bazar against the petitioner. 

 4. On receipt of the petition of complaint, the Magistrate examined the complainant under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and took cognizance of the offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and issued summon against the accused-petitioner. Thereafter the Magistrate issued warrant of arrest and subsequently published notice as per law. The case being triable by a court of Sessions the case record was sent to the Court of Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar and registered the case as ST Case No.1303 of 2014 for trial. That on 26-11-2014 the learned Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar framed charge against the accused under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. That the charge was framed in abstentia of the accused. 

 5. The prosecution examined two PW's and submitted some documents which were marked as Exhibits 1-9. Since the accused did not appear in the case, he could not be examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Sessions Judge on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record found the accused-petitioner guilty under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and convicted the petitioner and sentenced him to suffer imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay double amount of the face value of the 3 disputed cheques of Taka 80,00,000 with fine of Taka 1,60,00,000 (One crore, sixty lac). The complainant will get Taka 1,20,00,000 (one crore, twenty lac) out of the aforesaid amount of fine and rest of Taka 40,00,000 (Forty lac) will be deposited in the Government-Treasury. That the convict- petitioner was arrested on 2-1-2015 in connection with GR Case No. 2 of 2015 of Motijheel Police Station, Dhaka and he was sent to the jail hajat. That on 7-7-2015 the aforesaid fact was intimated to the Court of Sessions, Cox's Bazar and, as such, the accused was also shown arrested in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 vide Order No. 12 dated 7-7-2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge. 

 6. Thereafter, the petitioner preferred Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 before the Hon'ble High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh challenging the vires of section 138A of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 inserted vide section 3 of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2006 (২০০৬ সনের ৩ নং আইন) and the Judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by Court of Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar in ST Case No.1303 of 2014 arising out of CR Case No. 847 of 2013 of Senior Judicial Magistrate Court, Sadar, Cox's Bazar convicting the petitioner under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him to imprisonment for one year and a fine of Taka 1,60,00,000 (One crore sixty lac). 

 7. That after hearing on 14-12-2015, a Division Bench of the High Court Division was pleased to issue a Rule and further stay operation of the Judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by Court of Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 and further been pleased to enlarge the petitioner on bail for a period of 6 (six) weeks. That the order of stay and bail were extended from time to time. 

 8. That it is stated that thereafter the Hon'ble Chief Justice constituted a Full Bench comprising three judges of the Hon'ble High Court Division and sent Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 with other writ petitions to the Full Bench for hearing and disposal. That after hearing, their Lordships of the Full Bench of the High Court Division was pleased to discharge all the Rules vide judgment and order dated 7-9-2016. However, the Full Bench in the judgment observed that since the petitioner is claiming that the original CR case was not filed within the stipulated time of sending first demand notice and thus, proceedings of such CR case is liable to be quashed. But since this ground for adjudication is out of writ jurisdiction, the petitioner may raise this question under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before an appropriate Bench of this court and the petitioner was allowed to remain on the same bail as granted by this court upto 30th January, 2017. The petitioner is still enjoying the privilege of bail granted by the High Court Division. 

 9. After pronouncement of the Judgment by the Full Court of High Court Division on 7-9-2016 the convict-petitioner without filing an appeal provided under section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act again moved this court under section 561A against the same judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar, in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 arising out of CR Case No. 847 of 2013 of the Senior Judicial Magistrate Court, Sadar, Cox' Bazar convicting the petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 1,60,00,000 and obtained the present rule and stay. 

 10. This rule was contested by the opposite party No. 2 by filing Counter-Affidavit dated 3-8-2017 and Supplementary Affidavit dated 20-11-2017. In those affidavits opposite party No. 2 stated that after pronouncement of judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015, the petitioner earlier filed Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 challenging the provision of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, as well as judgment and order of conviction and sentence. The said writ petition with 55 writ petitions were heard together by Full Bench of the High Court Division and by majority decision the Rules were discharged. The Full Bench of the High Court Division found it needless to make any discussions on merit of the case of the petitioner, further observed that merit of the case against the petitioner has to be decided in appeal and not in the writ petition. Full Bench further observed that the petitioner may raise the question as to filing of original CR case after sending second legal notice under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before an appropriate Bench of the Hon'ble High Court Division. However, the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 is allowed to remain on bail which was granted by this court upto 30th January, 2017 for the purpose of 'filing a criminal miscellaneous case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is also alleged that after pronouncement of judgment and order of conviction and sentences remedy is available under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if it is found that the case in which conviction and sentences is passed is a case of no evidence, but the petitioner case do not come within such category. 

 13. At the out set, Mr Shah Md Munir Sharif, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the convict-petitioner submits that relying upon the judgment and order dated 7-9-2016 passed in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 by the Full Bench of the Hon'ble High Court Division, the petitioner filed the present application under section 561A for quashment of the judgment and order of conviction of the sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. He further submits that the conviction and sentence cannot be sustained as the complainant-payee could not create more than one cause of action in respect of the cheques and the complaint in question having been filed on the basis of the second presentation and resultant second cause of action was not maintainable. 

 14. He next submits that the trial court should have considered that the Second notice was served in contravention of statutory provision of law and filing the complaint petition under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not maintainable. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence of the Sessions Court is liable to be quashed. Learned Advocate by referring the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain reported in 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16 submits that if there is a legal bar against the initiation and continuation of the proceedings or the evidence adduced clearly and manifestly fails to prove the charge, an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is maintainable and in the instant case there is a legal bar against the initiation and continuation to the proceedings and the evidence clearly and manifestly fails to prove the charge, and therefore the instant application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is maintainable. 

 15. On the other hand, learned Advocate Mr Debashis Bhattachariya, appearing for the complainant-opposite party No. 2 vehemently submits that there is no scope for the convict petitioner to file an application under section 561A without following the mandatory provision laid down under section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act where there remains specific alternative remedy prescribed under section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 to file appeal against the judgment and order of conviction and sentences passed by the Sessions Judge subject to deposit of 50% of the dishonoured cheque amount before filing the appeal. He further submits that the decision of 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16 has referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner had no manner of application in the present case because of the facts that in the cited case proceeding was pending but in the present case there remained no proceedings and petitioner has been convicted by the Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar by the impugned judgment. In the present case complainant by adducing sufficient evidence has been able to prove his case and same was upheld by the Full Bench in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 and there is no scope to appraisal of the evidence sitting in the jurisdiction under section 561A. He next submits that the cheques were presented for encashment being dishonoured for insufficiency of fund, a notice of demand had been issued upon the petitioner within time contemplated under section 138(1) (b) and further complying all the legal formalities as laid down under section 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, petition of complaint has been filed. He lastly submits that the convict-petitioner filed the case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure only to delay and defeat the realisation of Taka 1,60,00,000 by the opposite-party No. 2. As such the petitioner has not come in clean hands and is not entitled to take shelter before this court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Accordingly learned Advocate prayed for discharge of the Rule with cost. 

 19. Upon hearing the learned Advocates of the parties, and perusal of the application it reveals that the following questions are to be decided in this case: 

 1.	Whether the petitioner can initiate present miscellaneous case challenging the conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed against him by the Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar in ST Case No. 1303 of 2014 arising CR Case No. 847 of 2013, convicting the petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him 1 year imprisonment and a fine of Taka 1,60,00,000, which was already decided in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 discharging the Rule by Full Bench of High Court Division by judgment dated 7-9-2016. 

 2.	Whether in the judgment and order passed by the Full Bench of High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 made any observation giving scope to the petitioner to file a criminal miscellaneous case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, where specific provision was made under section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act to file an appeal against the judgment and order of conviction passed by the sessions judge and in that case the convicted person must deposit 50% of the dishonoured amount before filing the appeal. 

 20. It appears that in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 one point for determination was whether the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by court of sessions are liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the other point was whether the provision of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 as inserted by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2006 is ultra vires the Constitution. The Full Bench of the High Court Division by its judgment dated 7-9-2016 held that there is no scope to challenge the judgment and order of conviction and sentence in writ jurisdiction and thus we find no merit in the argument of the learned Advocates for the petitioner relating to the legality of the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence accordingly, the Rules were discharged. However, on the prayer of the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015, the court observed that the petitioner Tofayel Ahmed, son of Abu Taher Bhuiyan is allowed to remain on the same bail as granted by this Court at the time of issuance of this Rule upto 30th January, 2017 so as to file a Criminal Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 24. Learned Advocate for the petitioner tried to submit that in the instant case legal notice under section 138(1)(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (as amended till date) issued twice upon the convict-petitioner, since the complainant-opposite party did not initiate the Petition of Complaint based on the first Legal Notice hence the proceedings initiated is not maintainable and thus the Judgment and Order of conviction and sentence is liable to be quashed. 

 26. That the convict-petitioner specifically alleges that, he received legal notices issued twice upon him and, as such, he had complete knowledge about the proceedings initiated against him but for the best reasons known to him he remained absent during trial, he did not even bother to appear before the trial court to raise such point as alleged by him. In exercising jurisdiction under section 561A this court cannot examine newly advance defence case not taken during trial. Since the convict-petitioner remained absent during the trial as such he waived right whatsoever to invoke the inherent power of the High Court Division conferred under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. In this application there is no necessity of making any discussion on merit of the case of the convict-petitioner. Whether there is merit or not in the sessions case against the petitioner has to be decided in appeal and not in this application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 28. In the case of Bangladesh vs Tan Kheng Hock reported in 31 DLR (AD) 69 our apex Court categorically held that "section 561A emphasises that the High Court has the jurisdiction to pass orders to secure the ends of justice and for that purpose that the High court is competent to entertain application not provided by the Code. However it must be clearly understood that the terms of section 561A of the Code do not extend the jurisdiction of the High Court Division to matters which are not inherently with that jurisdiction. The High Court also cannot claim inherent jurisdiction to exercise powers taken away by legislation. When exercising the jurisdiction, the High Court would no embark upon an enquiry whether the evidence in question is reliable or not." 

 29. Hence, since the legislature created forum of appeal by depositing 50% of the cheque amount challenging the Judgment and Order of conviction and sentence hence by way of such legislation, legislatures expressly curtailed the avenue to challenge the propriety of Judgment and Order of conviction and sentence passed in a case under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 without depositing 50% of the cheque amount and, as such, this instant Rule is liable to be discharged being not maintainable. 

 33. It is relevant to point out here that the petitioner have knowledge about the filing of the case. Primarily he challenged the judgment of order and sentence dated 29-4-2015 in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 but same was discharged by Full Bench of this Division on 7-9-2016. But without preferring appeal as provided under the special law, the petitioner again filed the present application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 3-11-2016 without stating any cause and reason in his application under section 561A of the said Code and not to pay his liability for Taka 80,00,000 which was admittedly received by him to sell of immovable property to the complainant-opposite-party No. 2. 

 34. Section 141, clause (c) of the Negotiable Instruments Act has provided for trial of such case by a senior Court, namely the Court of Sessions. Thereafter, by a subsequent amendment dated 9-2-2006, the earlier section 138A, regarding filing of appeal against the judgment of the trial Court, has also been replaced and substituted by a new section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act. In the new section, restriction has been imposed in preferring appeal against any order of sentence under section 138(1) of the Act unless an amount of not less then 50% of the amount of the dishonoured cheque is deposited before filing the appeal in the court which awarded the sentence, no appeal would be admissible. As such, the intention of the legislature is very much clear that the Negotiable Instruments Act, being a special law, special provision has been inserted to restrain lingering of the disposal of such cases and also to discourage preferring frivolous appeals. This piece of legislation by its nature is a beneficial one and the cheque-defaulter should not be indulged in a manner so that the legislative intent is allowed to be frustrated. 

 36. We have gone through the Judgment, oral evidence of PW's and the documents exhibited in the case. The learned Sessions Judge after considering the evidence of 3 PW's and materials on record rightly found that the drawer has failed to pay the amount shown in 3 cheques (Exhibit-2 series) within the stipulated period on receipt of legal notice issued under clause (b) of the section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and the complainant filed the complaint petition within the time prescribed as provided under section 141(b) of Negotiable Instruments Act. Thus it is evident that the trial court after consideration of the legal aspect and appreciating the oral and documentary evidence on record rightly found that the petitioner committed offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and accordingly convicted accused-petitioner and imposed fine of Taka 1,60,00,000. 

 37. In this connection we may also profitably refer the decision in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16 wherein their Lordship held: 

 "The settled principle of law is that to bring a case within the purview of section 561A for the purpose of quashing a proceeding one of following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 5) The allegations against the accused although constituted an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 38. Before parting, we must remember with great regret and shock that at the time of hearing of this case, learned Advocate Shah Md Munir Sharif appeared for the petitioner, but today when we are pronouncing judgment he is no more in this World. We remember and appreciate for his able assistance in conducting the case and remarkable contribution he afforded in the field of law. 

 39. In view of the discussion made above and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, provision of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, Judgment of the Full Bench of High Court Division dated 7-9-2016 in Writ Petition No. 12580 of 2015 and the decisions of our Apex Court reported in 28 DLR (AD) 28, 31 DLR (AD) 69, we do not find any merit in this Rule. 

 41. The conviction and sentence dated 29-4-2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Cox's Bazar in ST Case No. 1303 of 2004 arising out of CR Case No. 847 of 2003 of Senior Judicial Magistrate, Cox's Bazar convicting the convict-petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is affirmed.
